forces: Alto, solo violin, strings and continuo
performers: Hertha Töpper, alto; Otto Büchner, solo violin; Münchener Bach-Orchester; Karl Richter, conductor
question: How do a solo violin and an alto voice share one lament?
intro: This is the second selected highlight from the 1958 recording, not the whole Passion. After Peter’s denial, an alto and a solo violin answer in B minor; listen for how the violin’s opening music closes the aria.

sections.label: C · Violin link and Schaue hier
B′ · Erbarme dich returns
sections.mNote: opening words and key return after the middle section

sections.label: A′ · Ritornello again

cues.title: The aria alone
cues.text: This track begins with the aria itself; the narration of Peter’s denial is a separate track in the recording. The aria is for alto, solo violin, strings and continuo, in B minor and 12/8, and returns at the end to its opening violin music.
cues.evidence: The Internet Archive item lists the preceding recitative as its own track (No. 38b–c, 1:40) and this file begins with the violin. The Bach-Gesellschaft score (IMSLP 00935, printed pp. 168–172) shows a solo violin, violins I–II, viola, alto and continuo, 12/8 with two sharps, and ends with the instruction Dal Segno. Report: global key B minor; the sound starts near −31 dB and reaches −24 dB by 0:05.

cues.title: A violin sings first
cues.text: The solo violin carries the melody; the other violins and the viola sustain soft notes under it. The score marks them piano sempre — softly throughout — and marks the bass line pizzicato, plucked. The recorded level stays between −21 and −24 dB for the first half-minute.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score p. 168: ‘piano sempre’ under violins I–II and viola, ‘pizzicato’ at the continuo staff. Report: −23.8, −21.6, −24.3, −22.3, −23.0 and −24.2 dB at 0:05–0:30. The recording does not reveal whether the bass is plucked in this performance.

cues.title: The alto enters
cues.text: The ritornello closes on a fermata, a held chord, and the alto enters softly on ‘Erbarme dich’ — have mercy — at about 1:04. The level rises by roughly six decibels between 1:05 and 1:10 as the voice joins the violin and strings.
cues.evidence: Report: boundary 0.71 at 1:04; −21.7 dB at 1:00, −17.0 at 1:05, −10.5 at 1:10; onset rate from 3.2 to 6.0 per second. The score’s eight-bar introduction ends on a fermata and the voice enters marked pp (Bach-Gesellschaft score p. 168).

cues.title: Peter weeps
cues.text: Before the aria, Peter has denied Jesus three times; the cock crows and he goes out and weeps bitterly (Matthew 26:75). The aria’s poem, by Picander, ends on the same word: ‘Herz und Auge weint vor dir bitterlich’ — heart and eyes weep before you bitterly.
cues.evidence: The preceding recitative (No. 46 in the Bach-Gesellschaft numbering) ends ‘Und ging heraus und weinete bitterlich’; the aria text is printed in the Deutsche Grammophon booklet and on the Netherlands Bach Society page, https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-244, which names Picander as the poet.

cues.title: Violin and voice share the line
cues.text: While the alto sings, the solo violin keeps its own flowing figuration beside her. The words ‘Erbarme dich’ recur again and again, broken by rests. The report counts four to seven note onsets a second through this stretch, a busy texture under a slow pulse.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score pp. 168–170: the alto’s text repeats ‘er-bar-me dich’ with rests, and the solo violin staff carries running notes beside the voice. Report: onset rate between 4.2 and 7.0 per second in every window from 1:10 to 2:20.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bach, violinist
cues.text: Bach played the violin as well as the organ and keyboard instruments, and in this aria the violin has the first and last word. On the label of the LP side that carries the aria, the solo is credited to Otto Büchner.
cues.evidence: Instruments: this site’s Bach biography. The label of the Archiv Produktion LP side containing Nos. 42–53 (ARC 73 128 b, SAPM 198 628 b; Internet Archive LP item) lists Otto Büchner, violin. The aria’s opening and closing violin music is shown in the Bach-Gesellschaft score pp. 168 and 172.

cues.title: The first span closes
cues.text: Around 3:00–3:10 the pitch estimates turn to F♯ minor, the minor dominant, and the level falls to one of the quietest windows at 3:05. The alto pauses while the violin plays two bars alone; at about 3:15 the words change to ‘Schaue hier’ — look here — still quietly.
cues.evidence: Report: F♯ minor (r 0.86) at 3:00, (0.89) at 3:05 and (0.71) at 3:10; −15.6 dB at 3:00 and −24.4 at 3:05, one of the five quietest windows; boundaries 0.53 at 3:02 and 0.51 at 3:12; −17.7 to −20.1 dB at 3:15–3:25. Bach-Gesellschaft score p. 170 shows the alto resting for two bars after ‘um meiner Zähren willen’ while the violin plays, then ‘schau-e hier’ in bars 25–27, near 3:15 by proportion. Bar timing is not aligned.

cues.title: Weeping at full volume
cues.text: At 3:40 the level jumps by about ten decibels, and the strongest boundary of the whole aria falls at 3:54. By proportion the words are ‘Herz und Auge weint vor dir bitterlich’, and the loudest window of the aria, at 4:00, lies on them.
cues.evidence: Report: −19.4 dB at 3:35, −9.3 at 3:40, −4.0 at 4:00, the loudest window of the aria; boundaries 0.60 at 3:40 and 1.00 at 3:54. Bach-Gesellschaft score p. 171 sets ‘hier, Herz und Auge weint vor dir, weint vor dir bitterlich’ in bars 28–31, near 3:40–4:05 by proportion; the match is not aligned.

cues.title: Calls, then the opening returns
cues.text: From 4:05 the estimates sit on F♯ minor and the level falls to about −19 dB as ‘Erbarme dich’ is called repeatedly. Near 4:30 the alto restates the opening words in B minor; the level jumps from −17 to −7 dB by 4:40, and the pitch content resembles her first entry.
cues.evidence: Report: F♯ minor (r 0.75–0.86) from 4:10 to 4:35; −18.3 dB at 4:25, −19.0 at 4:30, −16.9 at 4:35, −7.0 at 4:40; B minor (0.77) at 4:40; boundaries 0.70 at 4:08 and 0.58 at 4:42. A comparison of the first entry (1:04–1:44) with every later window finds its best match near 4:30 (similarity 0.64 against an average of 0.54). Bach-Gesellschaft score p. 171 sets ‘er-bar-me dich’ repeatedly and the full opening words again in bars 34–36. Bar timing is by proportion.

cues.title: A passing G-major reading
cues.text: At 5:10 a single analysis window reads G major, built on the sixth step of B minor, before B minor returns at 5:15; one window cannot confirm a modulation. In the score the word ‘erbarme’ is stretched over a long run of notes about here.
cues.evidence: Report: G major (r 0.71) at 5:10 only, B minor (0.80 and 0.79) at 5:15 and 5:20; −11.6 dB at 5:10; the report warns that its key estimates are approximate. G is the sixth degree of B minor, and the estimate is not treated as a modulation. Bach-Gesellschaft score p. 172 has ‘er-bar----me’ extended through the third bar of the page (bar 39 by count), near 5:10–5:25 by proportion; the bar is not aligned.

cues.title: Bach’s own score
cues.text: The aria survives in Bach’s own hand: the autograph score of the revised Passion, Mus. ms. Bach P 25, is in the Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin. The Netherlands Bach Society dates the manuscript to 1736; the catalogue on IMSLP gives a range from 1736 to 1740.
cues.evidence: IMSLP, St Matthew Passion page: holograph manuscript, Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin, Mus. ms. Bach P 25, dated [1736–40] and 1740 in two entries; Netherlands Bach Society, https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-244, which says the manuscript of 1736 has been handed down.

cues.title: The last sung words
cues.text: Near 6:00 the harmony touches F♯, the dominant, once more, and by 6:25 it is back in B minor. The last sung words, ‘um meiner Zähren willen’ — for the sake of my tears — close the vocal part just before the violin returns.
cues.evidence: Report: loud window at 5:50 (−6.7 dB), −20.6 dB at 5:55 with F♯ major (r 0.66), bass F♯ at 6:00; B minor (0.77) at 6:25. Bach-Gesellschaft score p. 172 ends the vocal line on ‘um meiner Zähren willen’ with the instruction Dal Segno. The last words are located by score order, not aligned.

cues.title: The ritornello returns
cues.text: Near 6:32 the score’s Dal Segno sends the players back to the opening violin music. A comparison of the first minute with every later window finds its best match here (similarity 0.83 against an average of 0.62). The alto does not sing again.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score p. 172: Dal Segno. A comparison of 0:00–1:00 with every later window peaks at 6:32–6:33. Report: boundary 0.54 at 6:30 and 0.50 at 6:36; level −8.3 dB at 6:25, −20.0 at 6:30, −22.7 at 6:35.

cues.title: The opening, repeated
cues.text: The ritornello retraces its first path. The estimates lean to E minor around 6:45–6:55, as they did around 0:10–0:25, and again near 7:15–7:25, as they did around 0:45–0:55. Listen for the violin’s opening music coming back as written.
cues.evidence: Report: E minor (r 0.81, 0.76) at 6:45 and 6:50 and (0.72, 0.86, 0.78) at 7:15, 7:20 and 7:25, against E minor at 0:10–0:25 (0.73–0.84) and 0:45–0:55 (0.73–0.80) in the first ritornello. The offsets agree to within a few seconds.

cues.title: The last fermata
cues.text: The repeat runs to the ritornello’s fermata. The level falls from −12 dB at 7:30 to −31 dB at 7:40 and to about −49 dB in the final window. The chorale ‘Bin ich gleich von dir gewichen’ follows on the full recording; this selection does not include it.
cues.evidence: Report: −12.4 dB at 7:30, −18.9 at 7:35, −31.3 at 7:40, −49.4 at 7:45; B minor (0.91) at 7:35. The first ritornello also ends on a fermata (Bach-Gesellschaft score p. 168). The Internet Archive item lists the chorale as the next track (No. 40, 1:10).

transitions.title: A fermata, then the voice
transitions.how: The eight-bar ritornello ends with a fermata, a held chord that suspends the pulse. The alto then enters softly, marked pp, on ‘Erbarme dich’ while the violins and viola continue beneath in piano sempre. The solo violin does not stop: it keeps its flowing figuration beside the voice. The join is a pause and a change of texture rather than a new tempo, and the same B-minor music now carries words.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score p. 168: fermata in the eighth bar, ‘pp’ at the alto’s entry, ‘piano sempre’ in the strings. Report: boundary 0.71 at 1:04; level −21.7 dB at 1:00, −17.0 at 1:05, −10.5 at 1:10. The length of the fermata is not measured.

transitions.title: The voice stops; the violin speaks
transitions.to: C · Violin link and Schaue hier
transitions.how: The alto closes her first long statement on ‘um meiner Zähren willen’ and stops. By the pitch estimates the harmony has turned to F♯ minor, the minor dominant, and the level falls to one of the quietest windows of the track. The solo violin then plays alone for two bars while the alto rests; the new words, ‘Schaue hier’, arrive at about 3:15. The join is a link passage that hands the line from voice to violin and back, not a cadence into new material.
transitions.evidence: Report: F♯ minor (r 0.86–0.89) at 3:00–3:05; −15.6 dB at 3:00, −24.4 at 3:05; boundaries 0.53 at 3:02 and 0.51 at 3:12. Bach-Gesellschaft score p. 170: two bars of solo violin with the alto resting before ‘schau-e hier’. Key labels are estimates, not chord identifications.

transitions.title: Back to B minor by way of F♯
transitions.from: C · Violin link and Schaue hier
transitions.how: After the climax on ‘bitterlich’ the voice calls ‘Erbarme dich’ repeatedly over F♯ minor, the minor dominant, and the level drops to about −19 dB. The tonic is then restored as the alto restates the opening words in B minor; the level rises by about ten decibels within five seconds. The return is a retransition by way of the dominant: the music has travelled from B minor to F♯ and back, and the opening text comes back with it.
transitions.evidence: Report: F♯ minor (r 0.75–0.86) from 4:10 to 4:35, then B minor (0.77) at 4:40; −19.0 dB at 4:30, −16.9 at 4:35, −7.0 at 4:40; boundary 0.58 at 4:42. Bach-Gesellschaft score p. 171 sets ‘Erbarme dich, mein Gott, um meiner Zähren willen’ again in bars 34–36. The boundary time is approximate.

transitions.title: Dal Segno: the violin returns
transitions.how: The alto’s last phrase, ‘um meiner Zähren willen’, is followed by the instruction Dal Segno: the players return to the sign at the start and play the ritornello again, now without the voice. The recorded level falls from about −8 dB at 6:25 to −20 dB at 6:30, the violin’s opening music begins at about 6:32, and the second pass retraces the first minute’s harmonic path to the fermata.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score p. 172: Dal Segno. Report: −8.3 dB at 6:25, −20.0 at 6:30, −22.7 at 6:35; boundaries 0.54 at 6:30 and 0.50 at 6:36. A comparison of 0:00–1:00 with every later window peaks at 6:32–6:33, and the E-minor estimates recur at matching offsets.

source.title: Bach, Passionsmusik nach dem Evangelisten Matthäus (Matthäus-Passion), BWV 244, Bach-Gesellschaft Ausgabe, vol. 4, Zweiter Theil (Breitkopf & Härtel, 1854)
source.locator: No. 47, Aria (Coro I), printed pp. 168–172 (PDF pp. 36–40): Violino solo, Violino I, Violino II, Viola, Alto, and Organo e Continuo, ending Dal Segno. The recording’s booklet lists organ, cello, double bass and bassoon among the continuo players without assigning them to numbers, so the timeline shows the continuo as organ, cellos and basses. Entry times follow bar proportion and the report’s level changes; they are approximate.

timeline.note: The solo violin carries the ritornello’s melody over soft violins and viola (piano sempre); the score marks the bass pizzicato.
The alto enters, pp, on ‘Erbarme dich’; the solo violin keeps its flowing figuration beside her.
The alto rests for about two bars while the solo violin plays alone above the accompaniment.
The alto returns with ‘Schaue hier’, quietly, then rises to the climax on ‘bitterlich’.
The opening words ‘Erbarme dich, mein Gott’ return in B minor.
Dal Segno: the ritornello repeats without the voice and the aria closes on its fermata.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Hertha Töpper (alto), Otto Büchner (solo violin), Münchener Bach-Orchester (orchestra), Karl Richter (conductor)
fields.note: The booklet lists Hertha Töpper for the alto arias and Otto Büchner as the violinist. The label of the LP side that carries Nos. 42–53 credits both and does not assign Büchner to a single number; his identification as this aria’s solo violinist rests on that label and on the booklet naming no other violinist. The booklet also names continuo players for the whole Passion (organ Ekkehard Tietze and Hedwig Bilgram; double bass Franz Ortner; bassoon Karl Kolbinger; viola da gamba Oswald Uhl, whom Discogs also lists on continuo cello); which of them play in this aria is not stated, so they are not listed here.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The performing edition is not identified. The booklet numbers the aria 47 (the Bach-Gesellschaft and BWV numbering) while the Internet Archive and retail track titles number it 39 (the New Bach Edition). The file contains the aria alone: the preceding chorus and recitative ‘Wahrlich, du bist auch einer von denen — Da hub er an’ (booklet No. 46) is the previous track and the chorale ‘Bin ich gleich von dir gewichen’ is the next. The booklet gives the composition as Leipzig 1729 or earlier, revised 1736.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.value: 23 June – 21 August 1958 (sessions 23 June–6 July, 11–12 August and 21 August)
fields.note: The Archiv Produktion LP labels print the recording dates as 6/23–7/6, 8/11–12 and 21/1958; the retail page gives 23 June–6 July, 11–12 and 21 August 1958; the booklet essay gives 22 sessions between 23 June and 21 August 1958. Which session produced this aria is not stated.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Archiv Produktion (Deutsche Grammophon Gesellschaft, History of Music Division)
fields.note: The labels read ‘Archive Production — History of Music Division Deutsche Grammophon Ges.’ and ‘Stereo’.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: SAPM 198 009/012 (first stereo edition, four LPs); the scanned export pressing carries ARC 73 125–73 128 / SAPM 198 625–628, with this aria on the side labelled ARC 73 128 b / SAPM 198 628 b
fields.note: First release year is disputed in the sources: the booklet and Wikipedia say 1959 (the booklet reads ‘LPs released/veröffentlicht/paru 1959’ and prints ℗ 1959 Deutsche Grammophon); Discogs and the Internet Archive LP catalogue give 1958, which is the recording year. Both dates precede 1963. The digital file used here is a later remaster, not the LP.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: First stereo edition: fifth programme side of the set (Discogs side E), track E6 (7:44 on the LP); matrix and take numbers not read
fields.note: The side and position come from the Discogs tracklist, whose first edition is automatically coupled, so the programme side is not the physical side of a particular LP; the scanned export label for ‘No. 42–53 Trial in the Presence of Kaiphas and Pilate (24’26)’ is numbered 5 (ARC 73 128 b / SAPM 198 628 b). No run-out inscription was seen, so matrix and take are unknown.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No remastering engineer or studio is credited in the item metadata or the booklet. The booklet’s © 2001 Deutsche Grammophon notice and the retail page’s ‘Digitally remastered’ line show only that commercial digital releases exist. The upload is a private Internet Archive upload in the hifidelity collection.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is established. The Internet Archive item was created on 16 February 2026; that upload date is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: 24-bit/192 kHz FLAC (item description ‘1959 [FLAC 24-192]’), digitally remastered according to the retail page; streamed here through the Internet Archive’s VBR MP3 derivative.
fields.note: The item’s track titles and durations (7:46 for this track) match the retail page’s 2016 hi-res listing, so the file is probably that release, but the item names no source. No speed correction, noise reduction or restoration settings are stated.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Bach’s composition (d. 1750) and the Bach-Gesellschaft edition used for the orchestra view (Breitkopf & Härtel, 1854) are public domain.
fields.note: IMSLP catalogues the Bach-Gesellschaft volume as Public Domain. This does not clear the sound recording, the later remaster or the booklet’s prose.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: territorial — European recording-rights expiry; first publication documented before 1963 (Archiv Produktion stereo LP edition, 1958 or 1959).
fields.note: Programme rule 3. The recording was made in June–August 1958 and first issued on four stereo LPs; the booklet states 1959 and quotes a critic’s review of the four LPs from May 1959. Whether the first issue fell in 1958 or 1959, a recording published by 1959 had exhausted the ordinary EU 50-year phonogram term (to the end of 2009) before the extension that applied from 1 November 2013. This is territorial, not a licence: the Internet Archive item carries no licence URL and no Public Domain Mark. US status is not established and no US public-domain claim is made. The audio file is a later commercial digital remaster; this dossier relies on the first publication of the recording and does not separately clear any rights claimed in the remastering, which is a point for the integration lead.

composer.epithet: An organist, teacher and church musician who made a bass line, a dance rhythm and a fugue subject carry the same argument.
facts: Family musicians in Eisenach and Ohrdruf; school at Lüneburg; study of German, French and Italian scores
Arnstadt · Mühlhausen · Weimar · Köthen · Thomaskantor in Leipzig, 1723–50
Organ, harpsichord, clavichord and violin; an examiner of organs and a teacher of keyboard players
Cantatas, Passions, the B minor Mass, organ and keyboard cycles, concertos, unaccompanied string music
composer.background:
Bach was born into a family of professional musicians in Eisenach, where his father Johann Ambrosius served as a town musician. The surname already meant a trade: relatives supplied organists, cantors and instrumentalists across Thuringia. His mother died in 1694 and his father in 1695; at ten he went to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist in Ohrdruf who had studied with Pachelbel. Keyboard instruction belonged to that household, alongside school and choir. In 1700 Bach travelled to Lüneburg, where a place in the choir of St Michael’s school gave a boy without substantial means access to an education and a musical library.

The early career was practical and local. After a brief appointment at Weimar, he became organist of the New Church in Arnstadt in 1703, with a recently built instrument to test and play. His duties included working with students, and the town’s records preserve disputes over both his behaviour and his music. In 1705 he obtained leave to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck and stayed away much longer than authorised. Buxtehude’s organ works offered a model in which free passagework, recurring basses and strict counterpoint could occupy the same piece. Bach’s own organ preludes would retain that alternation between improvisatory display and composed argument.
